Arsenal Football Club]] is an English professional [[association football
column4: Holloway]], [[North London]], [[England]]. The first European football match played by Arsenal was against [[Stævnet
column5: Copenhagen XI]] on 25 September 1963. They have since participated in European club competitions on several occasions, most of which organised by the [[Union of European Football Associations]] (UEFA). Arsenal has won two European honours: the [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]] in [[1970 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup Final
column6: 1970]] and the [[European Cup Winners' Cup]] in [[1994 European Cup Winners' Cup Final
column7: 1994]] – the latter recognised by the European confederation. The club also reached the final of the [[UEFA Cup]] in [[2000 UEFA Cup Final
column8: 2000]] and became the first London team to appear in a [[UEFA Champions League]] final, in [[2006 UEFA Champions League Final

column1: Qualification for European club competitions is determined by a team's position in its domestic league, as well as how successfully a team fares in domestic cup competitions in the previous season. Following the [[Heysel Stadium disaster]] in 1985, UEFA placed an indefinite ban on all English teams from competing in Europe; the ban was lifted in the [[1991–92 European Cup
column2: 1991–92]] season, giving Arsenal the opportunity to play in the European Cup. From between [[1998–99 UEFA Champions League
column4: 2015–16]], Arsenal contested in eighteen successive UEFA Champions League seasons, a feat only surpassed by [[Real Madrid C.F.
column5: Real Madrid]] and shared with [[Manchester United F.C.
column6: Manchester United]]; this is a record in English football.

column1: Striker [[Thierry Henry]] holds the club record for most appearances with 89 and is the club's record goalscorer in European football with 42 goals. Arsenal's biggest winning margin in Europe is a 7–0 scoreline, this feat was achieved twice, firstly away at Standard Liege in the Cup Winners Cup and secondly a home victory against [[SK Slavia Prague
column2: Slavia Prague]] in the UEFA Champions League. Arsenal hold the European club competition record for the most consecutive clean sheets with ten between September 2005 and May 2006.
European Cup and UEFA Champions League history

column1: Club competitions between teams from different European countries can trace their origins as far back as 1897, when the Challenge Cup was created for clubs in the [[Austro-Hungarian Empire]], who did not meet under normal circumstances. The [[Sir Thomas Lipton Trophy]], named after entrepreneur and sportsman [[Thomas Lipton]], was established in 1909 and was contested between clubs from Italy, Great Britain, Germany and Switzerland; the competition lasted for two years.<ref>{{cite news
column2: title=BBC films story of World Cup winners
column9: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> The earliest attempt to create a cup for national champion clubs of Europe was made by Swiss club [[FC Servette]]. Founded in 1930, the [[Coupe des Nations]] featured clubs of ten major European football leagues and was deemed a success. Due to financial reasons, the competition was abandoned.<ref>''[[Nemzeti Sport]]'', 9 July 1930, p. 3.</ref>

column3: quote= ""The UEFA Cup is a consolation prize and the Cup Winners' Cup has been destroyed. Who plays in that now? Nobody. The fact is, the Champions' League is all-important. It is turning into a European League and over the next three or four years I think that will become more and more clear.""

column1: In December 1954, French sports magazine ''[[L'Equipe]]'' published an article by journalist and former professional footballer [[Gabriel Hanot]], who proposed the introduction of a European club competition.<ref name=""king"">{{cite book
column5: title=The European Ritual: Football in the New Europe
column10: isbn=0-7546-3652-6}}</ref> He initially suggested that each country should nominate a club to play in a mid-week European league; many clubs favoured a cup competition, which required less matches to play.<ref name=""king""/> A year later, ''L'Equipe'' sent out invitations to 18 clubs, selected by Hanot, Jacques Ferran and [[Jacques Goddet]], with UEFA agreeing to administrate the competition named as the [[European Champion Clubs' Cup]].<ref>{{cite book
column14: title=The European Ritual: Football in the New Europe
column19: isbn=0-7546-3652-6}}</ref> The [[European Cup Winners' Cup]], later retitled the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup, was founded in 1960 and involved the winning clubs of national cup competitions in Europe. Arsenal, in the [[Football League First Division
column20: First Division]] at the time, were ineligible for both competitions, given that the club did not win a league championship or domestic cup for almost two decades.<ref>{{cite web
column25: accessdate=16 July 2012 }}</ref> They however were invited to participate in the [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]], an annual European club competition which was set up to promote international trade fairs; where a club finished in their domestic league had no relevance to qualification as teams were selected from cities holding trade fairs. The Inter-Cities Fairs Cup was regarded as the predecessor to the [[UEFA Cup]], rebranded as the UEFA Europa League in 2008.<ref>{{cite news
column31: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Each competition round was staged over a [[two-legged tie]], with the winner determined by the [[aggregate score]]. The [[away goals rule]] is activated if the aggregate score is equal.<ref>{{cite web
column39: quote=If the two teams involved in a tie score the same number of goals over the two legs, the team which scores more away goals qualifies for the next stage.}}</ref>

column1: To reinvigorate the European Champion Clubs' Cup, the competition was expanded and rebranded as the UEFA Champions League in 1992. From the [[1997–98 UEFA Champions League
column2: 1997–98]] season, it was further expanded to include eight domestic league runners-up selected by a [[UEFA coefficient]] and preliminary spots the following season were awarded to the third placed team; in some leagues fourth from [[2002–03 UEFA Champions League
column3: 2002–03]]. The expansion and constant growth of the competition led to the decline of the Cup Winners' Cup, abolished in 1999 and by which point instigated proposals for a [[European Super League (association football)
column4: European Super League]]. [[Arsène Wenger]] has, on numerous occasions predicted the latter,<ref>{{cite news
column5: title=Wenger: European super league will happen
column13: title=European super league will be here in 10 years, says Arsène Wenger
column19: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> arguing the pressure of television companies will force it to happen: ""It's all about money. More games equal more money through TV revenue and I think the next few years will see not just two, but three or four teams from the top countries competing against each other. It's what television wants – big teams in big matches. That is why the Champions' League was introduced.""<ref>{{cite news
column20: title=Soccer – Wenger predicts even bigger Champions' League
column25: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Although Arsenal qualified for a fifteenth successive season of Champions League football in May 2012, this coincided with the club not winning a domestic honour since 2005, which led to open criticism over the competition's present format.<ref>{{cite news
column26: title=The chase for the Champions League dollars is breeding mediocrity
column33: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Wenger however has gone on to defend the club policy, stating a trophy for Arsenal is winning the Premier League or the Champions League; ""Would you like to finish tenth in the league but win the [[Football League Cup
column34: League Cup]] and say you have won a trophy? Certainly not.""<ref>{{cite news
column35: title=It's time for Arsenal to win trophies again, admits Arsène Wenger

column1: Arsenal first participated in European football during the [[1963–64 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup
column2: 1963–64]] season, via the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup. The competition was set up to promote international trade fairs in European cities, featuring clubs from cities playing in matches that hosted trade fairs. As London's representative, Arsenal was paired with Copenhagen team [[Copenhagen XI]] in the first round, played over [[two-legged tie
column8: page=10}}</ref> The first match ended in a 7–1 victory for Arsenal, with [[Geoff Strong]] and [[Joe Baker]] both scoring [[hat-trick]]s.<ref name=""first"">{{cite news
column9: title=Armadale winger hit Arsenal's first goal in Europe
column14: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Copenhagen XI won the second match 3–2, but lost 9–4 on aggregate. Arsenal faced [[Royal Football Club de Liège]] in the second round; the Belgian club won 4–2 on aggregate to progress into the quarter-finals.<ref>{{cite news
column15: title=Liege keep Arsenal on the run

column2: 1969–70]] season, Arsenal again participated in the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, after a six-year absence. Having beaten [[Glentoran F.C.
column3: Glentoran]] of Northern Ireland, Portugal's [[Sporting Lisbon]] and [[FC Rouen
column4: Rouen]] of France, Arsenal played Romanian club [[Dinamo Bacău]] in the quarter-finals. A 1–9 victory on aggregate saw the club progress into the last four, where they faced [[AFC Ajax
column12: page=23}}</ref> The pairing of both clubs pleased Arsenal manager [[Bertie Mee]], who wanted to play Ajax in the semi-finals to set up a possibility of meeting [[Inter Milan
column13: Internazionale]] in the final.<ref name=""Bertie""/> At Highbury in the first leg, Arsenal won 3–0 and restricted Ajax to a 1–0 win at the [[Olympic Stadium (Amsterdam)
column14: Olympisch Stadion]] to reach the final of the Fairs Cup.<ref name=""Ajax"">{{cite news
column15: title=Arsenal play it cool in defence
column21: page=23}}</ref> It was the fourth successive year the final featured an English club and the first for a London club.<ref name=""Ajax""/> Arsenal played Belgian opposition [[Anderlecht]] in the [[1970 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup Final]], played in the space of a week. Anderlecht won the first leg 3–1, with Arsenal midfielder [[Ray Kennedy]] scoring a crucial [[Away goals rule
column22: away goal]], seven minutes from the final whistle.<ref>{{cite news
column29: page=33}}</ref> An early goal scored by [[Eddie Kelly (footballer)
column30: Eddie Kelly]] helped Arsenal to what earlier looked to be an improbable victory; [[John Radford (footballer)
column31: John Radford]] and [[Jon Sammels]] overturned Anderlecht's advantage to win 3–0 on the night and 4–3 on aggregate.<ref>{{cite web
column36: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> The result ended Arsenal's 17-year wait for a trophy and ensured the club became the third successive English club to win the honour.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal entered the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup the following season as holders of the competition, but did not progress further than the semi-finals, losing on away goals to [[1. FC Köln]] of Germany.<ref>{{cite news
column8: page=23}}</ref> The club did however win the league championship for the first time in 18 years, ensuring qualification for the [[UEFA Champions League
column9: European Champions Clubs' Cup]] in the 1971–72 season.<ref>{{cite news
column16: page=19}}</ref> Arsenal reached the quarter-finals, where the team lost to holders Ajax, who went on to retain the trophy.<ref>{{cite news
column23: page=27}}</ref> In subsequent seasons, the departure of Mee and lack of domestic honours meant that the club did not contest in European football.

column1: Mee was succeeded by [[Terry Neill]] in July 1976. Arsenal returned to European club football in the [[1978–79 UEFA Cup
column2: 1978–79]] season, having finished fifth in the previous league campaign. The club contested in the [[UEFA Cup]] for the first time and won their opening leg 3–0 against [[1. FC Lokomotive Leipzig]]; a commanding performance away from home in the second leg allowed Arsenal to win 1–4 at the [[Bruno-Plache-Stadion]] and 7–1 on aggregate.<ref>{{cite news
column9: page=22}}</ref> Arsenal progressed past the third round, winning on aggregate against [[Hajduk Split]] but were eliminated by [[Red Star Belgrade]] in the third round after striker [[Dušan Savić]] scored an away goal, two minutes from the end of the match.<ref>{{cite news
column10: title=Ten men go down at the very end

column1: As winners of the [[1979 FA Cup Final]], Arsenal entered the [[European Cup Winners' Cup]] in the [[1979–80 European Cup Winners' Cup
column3: Fenerbahçe]], [[1. FC Magdeburg]] and [[IFK Göteborg]], before facing [[Juventus F.C.
column4: Juventus]] in the semi-finals. After conceding an early penalty scored by [[Antonio Cabrini]], Arsenal defender [[David O'Leary]] was injured and substituted in the 20th minute, when Juventus striker [[Roberto Bettega]] tackled him.<ref name=""Juv"">{{cite news
column11: page=20}}</ref> [[Marco Tardelli]] was later sent off for a foul on [[Liam Brady]] and in the 85th minute, Arsenal managed to score an equaliser through a mix-up between [[Frank Stapleton]] and Bettega; the Italian put the ball into his goal net.<ref name=""Juv""/> Neill in his post-match comments expressed his anger over Bettega's tackle after the game: ""I was shocked by a most vicious foul. I was shocked because I have always had the greatest admiration for him.""<ref name=""Juv""/> A headed goal by substitute [[Paul Vaessen]] two minutes from the end, in the second leg was enough to take Arsenal into the [[1980 European Cup Winners' Cup Final]], where they faced [[Valencia CF
column19: page=24}}</ref> A goalless draw after normal and extra time meant the final was to be decided on a penalty shootout, with Valencia winning 5–4.<ref>{{cite news

column3: 1982–83]] seasons and departed in the first and second round to [[K.R.C. Genk
column5: Spartak Moscow]] respectively. The [[Heysel Stadium disaster]] of May 1985, during the [[1985 European Cup Final]] between [[Liverpool F.C.
column6: Liverpool]] and Juventus resulted in UEFA, and later [[FIFA]], imposing a 'worldwide' ban on English teams from participating in European club competitions, initially for an indefinite period.<ref>{{cite news
column18: George Graham]], Arsenal returned to the European Cup in the 1991–92 season, having won the league championship a season earlier.<ref>{{cite news
column25: page=16}}</ref> They went out in the second round to Portuguese team [[S.L. Benfica
column33: page=18}}</ref> The ban arising from the Heysel disaster had prevented Arsenal from competing in the European Cup when they won the league title two years previously, as well as preventing them from competing in the UEFA Cup on two occasions.

column1: In the [[1993–94 European Cup Winners' Cup
column2: 1993–94]] season, Arsenal contested in the European Cup Winners' Cup, having won the [[1993 FA Cup Final]]. The club beat [[Odense BK]] and [[Standard Liège]] to reach the quarter-finals, with the latter described as a ""breathtaking performance"" by Graham, after winning 7–0 at the [[Stade Maurice Dufrasne]].<ref>{{cite news
column10: Torino]] of Italy and French representative [[Paris Saint-Germain]] to reach the [[1994 European Cup Winners' Cup Final]] alongside [[Parma F.C.

column18: page=16}}</ref> Although Parma began the match the strongest of both teams, Arsenal opened the scoring through a well taken volley by striker [[Alan Smith (footballer born 1962)
column19: Alan Smith]]. Defending in numbers, the team held on to record an improbable victory and win the club's second European trophy, after a 24-year wait.<ref>{{cite news
column26: page=22}}</ref> After the match Graham praised his team's performance and defended his pragmatic approach; ""Sometimes we could go forward a little bit more and entertain a bit more, but we play to our strengths, like we did in this match. There's nothing wrong with having a very, very good defence, believe me. We've proved it, and it's a big plus.""<ref>{{cite news

Arsenal Football Club]] is an English professional [[association football
column4: Holloway]], [[North London]], [[England]]. The first European football match played by Arsenal was against [[Stævnet

They have since participated in European club competitions on several occasions, most of which organised by the [[Union of European Football Associations]] (UEFA). Arsenal has won two European honours: the [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]] in [[1970 Inter-Cities Fairs Cup Final
column6: 1970]] and the [[European Cup Winners' Cup]] in [[1994 European Cup Winners' Cup Final
column7: 1994]] – the latter recognised by the European confederation. The club also reached the final of the [[UEFA Cup]] in [[2000 UEFA Cup Final

column1: Qualification for European club competitions is determined by a team's position in its domestic league, as well as how successfully a team fares in domestic cup competitions in the previous season. Following the [[Heysel Stadium disaster]] in 1985, UEFA placed an indefinite ban on all English teams from competing in Europe; the ban was lifted in the [[1991–92 European Cup
column2: 1991–92]] season, giving Arsenal the opportunity to play in the European Cup. From between [[1998–99 UEFA Champions League
column4: 2014–15]], Arsenal contested in seventeen successive UEFA Champions League seasons, a feat only surpassed by [[Real Madrid C.F.

column1: Striker [[Thierry Henry]] holds the club record for most appearances with 89 and is the club's record goalscorer in European football with 42 goals. Arsenal's biggest winning margin in Europe is a 7–0 scoreline, this feat was achieved twice, firstly away at Standard Liege in the Cup Winners Cup and secondly a home victory against [[SK Slavia Prague
column2: Slavia Prague]] in the UEFA Champions League. Arsenal hold the European club competition record for the most consecutive clean sheets with ten between September 2005 and May 2006.
European Cup and UEFA Champions League history

column1: Club competitions between teams from different European countries can trace their origins as far back as 1897, when the Challenge Cup was created for clubs in the [[Austro-Hungarian Empire]], who did not meet under normal circumstances. The [[Sir Thomas Lipton Trophy]], named after entrepreneur and sportsman [[Thomas Lipton]], was established in 1909 and was contested between clubs from Italy, Great Britain, Germany and Switzerland; the competition lasted for two years.<ref>{{cite news
column2: title=BBC films story of World Cup winners
column9: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> The earliest attempt to create a cup for national champion clubs of Europe was made by Swiss club [[FC Servette]]. Founded in 1930, the [[Coupe des Nations]] featured clubs of ten major European football leagues and was deemed a success. Due to financial reasons, the competition was abandoned.<ref>''[[Nemzeti Sport]]'', 9 July 1930, p. 3.</ref>

column1: In December 1954, French sports magazine ''[[L'Equipe]]'' published an article by journalist and former professional footballer [[Gabriel Hanot]], who proposed the introduction of a European club competition.<ref name=""king"">{{cite book
column5: title=The European Ritual: Football in the New Europe
column10: isbn=0-7546-3652-6}}</ref> He initially suggested that each country should nominate a club to play in a mid-week European league; many clubs favoured a cup competition, which required less matches to play.<ref name=""king""/> A year later, ''L'Equipe'' sent out invitations to 18 clubs, selected by Hanot, Jacques Ferran and [[Jacques Goddet]], with UEFA agreeing to administrate the competition named as the [[European Champion Clubs' Cup]].<ref>{{cite book
column14: title=The European Ritual: Football in the New Europe
column19: isbn=0-7546-3652-6}}</ref> The [[European Cup Winners' Cup]], later retitled the UEFA Cup Winners' Cup, was founded in 1960 and involved the winning clubs of national cup competitions in Europe. Arsenal, in the [[Football League First Division
column20: First Division]] at the time, were ineligible for both competitions, given that the club did not win a league championship or domestic cup for almost two decades.<ref>{{cite web
column25: accessdate=16 July 2012 }}</ref> They however were invited to participate in the [[Inter-Cities Fairs Cup]], an annual European club competition which was set up to promote international trade fairs; where a club finished in their domestic league had no relevance to qualification as teams were selected from cities holding trade fairs. The Inter-Cities Fairs Cup was regarded as the predecessor to the [[UEFA Cup]], rebranded as the UEFA Europa League in 2008.<ref>{{cite news
column31: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Each competition round was staged over a [[two-legged tie]], with the winner determined by the [[aggregate score]]. The [[away goals rule]] is activated if the aggregate score is equal.<ref>{{cite web
column39: quote=If the two teams involved in a tie score the same number of goals over the two legs, the team which scores more away goals qualifies for the next stage.}}</ref>

column1: To reinvigorate the European Champion Clubs' Cup, the competition was expanded and rebranded as the UEFA Champions League in 1992. From the [[1997–98 UEFA Champions League
column2: 1997–98]] season, it was further expanded to include eight domestic league runners-up selected by a [[UEFA coefficient]] and preliminary spots the following season were awarded to the third placed team; in some leagues fourth from [[2002–03 UEFA Champions League
column3: 2002–03]]. The expansion and constant growth of the competition led to the decline of the Cup Winners' Cup, abolished in 1999 and by which point instigated proposals for a [[European Super League (association football)
column4: European Super League]]. [[Arsène Wenger]] has, on numerous occasions predicted the latter,<ref>{{cite news
column5: title=Wenger: European super league will happen
column13: title=European super league will be here in 10 years, says Arsène Wenger
column19: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> arguing the pressure of television companies will force it to happen: ""It's all about money. More games equal more money through TV revenue and I think the next few years will see not just two, but three or four teams from the top countries competing against each other. It's what television wants – big teams in big matches. That is why the Champions' League was introduced.""<ref>{{cite news
column20: title=Soccer – Wenger predicts even bigger Champions' League
column25: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Although Arsenal qualified for a fifteenth successive season of Champions League football in May 2012, this coincided with the club not winning a domestic honour since 2005, which led to open criticism over the competition's present format.<ref>{{cite news
column26: title=The chase for the Champions League dollars is breeding mediocrity
column33: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Wenger however has gone on to defend the club policy, stating a trophy for Arsenal is winning the Premier League or the Champions League; ""Would you like to finish tenth in the league but win the [[Football League Cup
column34: League Cup]] and say you have won a trophy? Certainly not.""<ref>{{cite news
column35: title=It's time for Arsenal to win trophies again, admits Arsène Wenger

column15: title=Liege keep Arsenal on the run

column12: page=23}}</ref> The pairing of both clubs pleased Arsenal manager [[Bertie Mee]], who wanted to play Ajax in the semi-finals to set up a possibility of meeting [[Inter Milan

Anderlecht won the first leg 3–1, with Arsenal midfielder [[Ray Kennedy]] scoring a crucial [[Away goals rule

column1: Arsenal entered the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup the following season as holders of the competition, but did not progress further than the semi-finals, losing on away goals to [[1. FC Köln]] of Germany.<ref>{{cite news
column8: page=23}}</ref> The club did however win the league championship for the first time in 18 years, ensuring qualification for the [[UEFA Champions League
column9: European Champions Clubs' Cup]] in the 1971–72 season.<ref>{{cite news
column16: page=19}}</ref> Arsenal reached the quarter-finals, where the team lost to holders Ajax, who went on to retain the trophy.<ref>{{cite news
column23: page=27}}</ref> In subsequent seasons, the departure of Mee and lack of domestic honours meant that the club did not contest in European football.

column1: Mee was succeeded by [[Terry Neill]] in July 1976. Arsenal returned to European club football in the [[1978–79 UEFA Cup
column2: 1978–79]] season, having finished fifth in the previous league campaign. The club contested in the [[UEFA Cup]] for the first time and won their opening leg 3–0 against [[1. FC Lokomotive Leipzig]]; a commanding performance away from home in the second leg allowed Arsenal to win 1–4 at the [[Bruno-Plache-Stadion]] and 7–1 on aggregate.<ref>{{cite news
column9: page=22}}</ref> Arsenal progressed past the third round, winning on aggregate against [[Hajduk Split]] but were eliminated by [[Red Star Belgrade]] in the third round after striker [[Dušan Savić]] scored an away goal, two minutes from the end of the match.<ref>{{cite news
column10: title=Ten men go down at the very end

column1: As winners of the [[1979 FA Cup Final]], Arsenal entered the [[European Cup Winners' Cup]] in the [[1979–80 European Cup Winners' Cup
column3: Fenerbahçe]], [[1. FC Magdeburg]] and [[IFK Göteborg]], before facing [[Juventus F.C.
column4: Juventus]] in the semi-finals. After conceding an early penalty scored by [[Antonio Cabrini]], Arsenal defender [[David O'Leary]] was injured and substituted in the 20th minute, when Juventus striker [[Roberto Bettega]] tackled him.<ref name=""Juv"">{{cite news
column11: page=20}}</ref> [[Marco Tardelli]] was later sent off for a foul on [[Liam Brady]] and in the 85th minute, Arsenal managed to score an equaliser through a mix-up between [[Frank Stapleton]] and Bettega; the Italian put the ball into his goal net.<ref name=""Juv""/> Neill in his post-match comments expressed his anger over Bettega's tackle after the game: ""I was shocked by a most vicious foul. I was shocked because I have always had the greatest admiration for him.""<ref name=""Juv""/> A headed goal by substitute [[Paul Vaessen]] two minutes from the end, in the second leg was enough to take Arsenal into the [[1980 European Cup Winners' Cup Final]], where they faced [[Valencia CF
column19: page=24}}</ref> A goalless draw after normal and extra time meant the final was to be decided on a penalty shootout, with Valencia winning 5–4.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal competed in the UEFA Cup in the [[1981–82 UEFA Cup
column3: 1982–83]] seasons and departed in the first and second round to [[K.R.C. Genk
column5: Spartak Moscow]] respectively. The [[Heysel Stadium disaster]] of May 1985, during the [[1985 European Cup Final]] between [[Liverpool F.C.
column6: Liverpool]] and Juventus resulted in UEFA, and later [[FIFA]], imposing a 'worldwide' ban on English teams from participating in European club competitions, initially for an indefinite period.<ref>{{cite news
column18: George Graham]], Arsenal returned to the European Cup in the 1991–92 season, having won the league championship a season earlier.<ref>{{cite news
column25: page=16}}</ref> They went out in the second round to Portuguese team [[S.L. Benfica
column33: page=18}}</ref> The ban arising from the Heysel disaster had prevented Arsenal from competing in the European Cup when they won the league title two years previously, as well as preventing them from competing in the UEFA Cup on two occasions.

column1: In the [[1993–94 European Cup Winners' Cup
column2: 1993–94]] season, Arsenal contested in the European Cup Winners' Cup, having won the [[1993 FA Cup Final]]. The club beat [[Odense BK]] and [[Standard Liège]] to reach the quarter-finals, with the latter described as a ""breathtaking performance"" by Graham, after winning 7–0 at the [[Stade Maurice Dufrasne]].<ref>{{cite news
column10: Torino]] of Italy and French representative [[Paris Saint-Germain]] to reach the [[1994 European Cup Winners' Cup Final]] alongside [[Parma F.C.
column11: Parma]], staged at Copenhagen. Without top goalscorer [[Ian Wright]] and markers [[John Jensen]] and [[Martin Keown]], Arsenal went into the final as outsiders.<ref>{{cite news
column18: page=16}}</ref> Although Parma began the match the strongest of both teams, Arsenal opened the scoring through a well taken volley by striker [[Alan Smith (footballer born 1962)
column19: Alan Smith]]. Defending in numbers, the team held on to record an improbable victory and win the club's second European trophy, after a 24-year wait.<ref>{{cite news
column26: page=22}}</ref> After the match Graham praised his team's performance and defended his pragmatic approach; ""Sometimes we could go forward a little bit more and entertain a bit more, but we play to our strengths, like we did in this match. There's nothing wrong with having a very, very good defence, believe me. We've proved it, and it's a big plus.""<ref>{{cite news
column27: title=Graham proud of his very English coup

column1: As holders of the competition, Arsenal was admitted into the Cup Winners' Cup for the [[1994–95 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup
column2: 1994–95]] season. They moreover contested in the [[1994 European Super Cup]], losing to [[A.C. Milan
column8: page=1}}</ref> In February 1995, Graham was sacked by Arsenal after it emerged he accepted an illegal £425,000 payment from Norwegian agent [[Rune Hauge]] for two of his clients: Jensen and [[Pål Lydersen]].<ref>{{cite news
column17: page=1}}</ref> He was replaced by caretaker manager [[Stewart Houston]] ([[Bruce Rioch]] in the close season), who managed to take Arsenal into the [[1995 UEFA Cup Winners' Cup Final]] after beating [[U.C. Sampdoria
column18: Sampdoria]] on penalties in the semi-finals.<ref>{{cite news
column25: page=22}}</ref> They however, did not retain the trophy after [[Real Zaragoza]] midfielder [[Nayim]] scored an extra-time goal, lobbing Arsenal goalkeeper [[David Seaman]].<ref>{{cite news

column1: In August 1996, Rioch was dismissed by Arsenal. He was replaced by [[Arsène Wenger]], who became the club's first manager born outside the British Isles. Wenger had creditable experience in UEFA club competitions; at Monaco he reached the final of the Cup Winners' Cup in 1992, losing 2–0 to [[Werder Bremen]] and took the club into the semi-finals of the European Cup in 1993–94. Wenger wanted Arsenal to become one of the biggest clubs in Europe, emphasising on buying talent from all over the world and patience shown by the club's board and supporters.<ref>{{cite book
column5: title=Successful Change Management: The Fifty Key Facts
column11: isbn=0-8264-7205-2}}</ref> His first involvement in a European match for Arsenal was against [[Borussia Mönchengladbach]] on 26 September 1996 in the UEFA Cup; Arsenal lost 6–4 on aggregate.<ref>{{cite news
column12: title=Arsenal's dreams are ended by Juskowiak
column19: accessdate=21 May 2012 }}</ref> Having watched the game from the stands in the first half, he assumed control in the second, suggesting the formation should accommodate four defenders instead of five.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal finished third in the [[1996–97 FA Premier League
column2: 1996–97]] league season, missing out on qualification for the UEFA Champions League by goal difference.<ref>{{cite news
column3: title=Football: Three Gunner salute for Baseball Ground
column10: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> They, however qualified for the UEFA Cup first round, but lost to [[PAOK Salonika]] of Greece over two legs in September 1997.<ref>{{cite news
column11: title=Greeks' late goal sends Arsenal tumbling out
column18: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal completed the double in the [[1997–98 Arsenal F.C. season
column19: 1997–98]] season, and winning the league ensured the club participated in the Champions League for the first time since its rebranding in 1992.<ref>{{cite news
column20: title=Gunners rest their case for the defence
column26: page=A3}}</ref> To benefit from increased revenue and higher attendances, Arsenal was granted permission from the Football Association and UEFA to host their home Champions League matches at [[Wembley Stadium (1923)

column1: The club faced French champions [[RC Lens
column4: Panathinaikos]] of Greece in the group stages of the competition.<ref>{{cite news
column10: publisher=BBC}}</ref> Although they began the campaign in good stead, with two draws and a win, Arsenal lost 3–1 to Dynamo Kiev and at home to Lens – watched by a record crowd of 73,707, meaning the club could not reach higher than third place, failing to make the quarter-finals.<ref>{{cite news
column18: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal ended the [[1998–99 FA Premier League
column19: 1998–99]] league season as runners-up, qualifying for the group stages of the Champions League for the second successive year.<ref>{{cite news
column25: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Again, Arsenal finished in third spot in their group, this time behind Barcelona and [[ACF Fiorentina
column32: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> The team, however advanced into the UEFA Cup third round and Arsenal chose to revert to playing their home matches at Highbury, on the advice of the players.<ref>{{cite news
column40: accessdate=22 May 2012 }} {{subscription required}}</ref> Arsenal beat [[FC Nantes
column41: Nantes]] and [[Deportivo de La Coruña]] over two legs and defeated Werder Bremen in the quarter-final; midfielder Ray Parlour scored a hat-trick in the second leg.<ref>{{cite news
column46: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> In the semi-final against Lens, Arsenal secured a 3–1 aggregate win to face Turkish opposition [[Galatasaray S.K. (football team)
column47: Galatasaray]] in the final, who beat [[Leeds United A.F.C.
column50: title=Arsenal left to fly Euro flag

column1: At Copenhagen, the venue for the [[2000 UEFA Cup Final]], both Arsenal and Galatasaray played out to a goalless draw in normal and in extra time. Arsenal lost 4–1 in a penalty shootout, with striker [[Davor Šuker]] and midfielder [[Patrick Vieira]] hitting the post and underside of the crossbar respectively.<ref name=""Gala"">{{cite news
column2: title=Football: Not Again; First Nayim, now it's Popescu. Arsenal's Euro dream is wrecked by the curse of Spurs Arsenal 0 Galatasaray 0 UEFA Cup final: Arsenal lose 4–1 on penalties
column9: accessdate=22 May 2012 }} {{subscription required}}</ref> Wenger reflected on the defeat by saying, ""We did not play well in the first half, but we were much better afterwards. It is very disappointing.""<ref name=""Gala""/> The final was overshadowed by events at the city centre, where Arsenal supporter Paul Dineen was stabbed in the back.<ref name=""fight"">{{cite news
column15: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> Referred to as the ""[[2000 UEFA Cup Final riots
column16: Battle of Copenhagen]]"", the incident escalated into a riot between English and Turkish fans, forcing the Danish police to use tear gas in order to restore calm.<ref name=""fight""/><ref>{{cite news
column17: title=Free to riot at Euro 2000: The Battle of Copenhagen; Anger as Danes send 19 English hooligans home without charge

column4: A sign outside Highbury, displaying the upcoming Arsenal—Internazionale match in September 2003.]]

column1: Arsenal qualified for the group stages of the Champions League in the [[2000–01 Arsenal F.C. season
column2: 2000–01]] season, having ended the previous league season in second.<ref>{{cite news
column10: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> The club won their first three matches in Group B, against [[AC Sparta Prague
column14: title=Lazio cop a lacing from Ljungberg
column21: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> A draw away to Lazio at the [[Stadio Olimpico]] ensured qualification into the second group stage, where they were partnered with Bayern Munich, Lyon and [[FC Spartak Moscow
column28: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> In spite of defender [[Sylvinho]] scoring an early goal in their opening game against Spartak Moscow, Arsenal plummeted to a 4–1 defeat, leaving Wenger to assess that ""as a team, we didn't look as solid as we are used to.""<ref>{{cite news
column36: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> Wins at Lyon and at home to Spartak Moscow helped Arsenal to qualify for the quarter-finals as the French club failed to capitalise on Arsenal's defeat at Bayern Munich.<ref>{{cite news
column42: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> They faced Spanish club Valencia, winning 2–1 at Highbury but the team were beaten 1–0 at the [[Estadio Mestalla]], knocked-out on aggregate.<ref>{{cite news

column2: 2001–02]] season, Arsenal played in the Champions League. The club qualified for the second group stage on goal difference but did not reach the quarter-finals, losing their final two matches against Deportivo La Coruña and Juventus.<ref>{{cite news
column8: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Having won the domestic league for the first time in four years, Wenger revealed the club's and his own intent to win the Champions League, telling French newspaper ''L'Equipe'' ""I can't imagine finishing my life without winning the European Cup"".<ref>{{cite news
column16: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal began the [[2002–03 UEFA Champions League
column17: following season]] impressively, winning 0–4 at [[PSV Eindhoven]].<ref>{{cite news
column18: title=Quick Silva starts Arsenal goal rush
column25: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> The match set a new club record, as midfielder [[Gilberto Silva]] scored the fastest goal, in 20.07 seconds.<ref>{{cite news
column33: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> Although Arsenal lost their last two matches against [[Borussia Dortmund]] and [[AJ Auxerre
column34: Auxerre]], coinciding with a blip in form domestically, they qualified for the second group stage for the third consecutive season.<ref>{{cite news
column35: title=Gunners happy to draw a blank
column42: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Striker [[Thierry Henry]] scored his first hat-trick in Europe for Arsenal against [[A.S. Roma
column43: Roma]] on 27 November 2002 with the player stating; ""It's wonderful to score a hat-trick but it's even more important that I did so in a game we've won.""<ref>{{cite news
column44: title=Football: Emperor of Rome; Roma 1 Arsenal 3: Henry rocks Italians with historic treble
column50: date=28 November 2002
column51: accessdate=23 May 2012 }} {{subscription required}}</ref> Arsenal failed to replicate their form at Roma, drawing their next four matches and losing to Valencia in the final match to finish third in their group and thus, out of the competition.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal entered the Champions League group stage in the [[2003–04 UEFA Champions League
column2: 2003–04]] season and faced Dynamo Kiev, [[Inter Milan
column4: Lokomotiv Moscow]]. Without a win in their first three matches, Arsenal faced an early exit from the competition but managed a victory against Dynamo Kiev, after defender [[Ashley Cole]] scored via a header.<ref>{{cite news
column12: accessdate=25 May 2012 }}</ref> At the [[San Siro]], Arsenal beat Internazionale 1–5, in a performance described as ""one of the greatest results in [the club's] history"".<ref>{{cite news
column20: accessdate=23 May 2012 }}</ref> A win in their final group game against Lokomotiv Moscow was enough for Arsenal to top their group and play an unseeded team in the last 16. Arsenal eliminated [[Celta de Vigo
column21: Celta Vigo]] and faced fellow English club [[Chelsea F.C.
column22: Chelsea]] at the quarter-final stage. Going into the first leg, Arsenal were favourites, having played their London rivals three times during the course the season, winning each occasion.<ref>{{cite news
column28: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> Former Dutch international [[Johan Cruyff]] backed Arsenal to win the competition, saying ""If Arsenal win it playing football the way only they know how then Europe would be proud to have such champions"".<ref>{{cite news
column34: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> In spite of [[Robert Pirès]] scoring a vital away goal at [[Stamford Bridge (stadium)
column35: Stamford Bridge]], Chelsea beat Arsenal 1–2 at Highbury to progress into the semi-finals.<ref>{{cite news
column36: title=Bridge's late decider leaves Arsenal dreams in shreds
column43: accessdate=24 May 2012 }}</ref> A year later, Arsenal exited the Champions League after losing 2–3 to Bayern Munich on aggregate, in the last 16 stage.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal qualified for the group stages of the Champions League in the [[2005–06 UEFA Champions League
column2: 2005–06]] season, finishing first in a group containing Ajax, Sparta Prague and [[FC Thun
column3: Thun]]. The club faced [[Real Madrid C.F.
column4: Real Madrid]] in the last 16; a solo goal by Henry at the [[Estadio Santiago Bernabéu]] in the first leg inflicted the home team's first defeat in 18 Champions League matches.<ref>{{cite news
column5: title=Henry storms Real citadel to reignite Gunners
column12: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal produced a disciplined display at home a fortnight after to reach the quarter-finals and become the sole English representative left in the competition.<ref>{{cite news
column13: title=Proud Arsenal carry the flag for England
column20: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> At home to Juventus, Arsenal won 2–0, and a goalless draw at the [[Stadio delle Alpi]] meant the club progressed into the semi-finals against [[Villarreal CF
column22: title=Arsenal hold nerve as Nedved sees red
column29: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> In the club's final European match at Higbhury, [[Kolo Touré]] scored a first-half winner to give Arsenal a 1–0 win.<ref>{{cite news
column30: title=Arsenal bring Highbury curtain down in style

column8: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> A late penalty save by goalkeeper [[Jens Lehmann]] in the second leg sent Arsenal into the [[2006 UEFA Champions League Final]], staged at the [[Stade de France]], Paris.<ref>{{cite news
column9: title=Lehmann the hero as Arsenal triumph
column16: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> The result, another goalless draw, was Arsenal's tenth [[clean sheet]] in a row – a new competition record.<ref>{{cite news
column17: title=Lehmann a saviour from the spot as Arsenal pack their bags for Paris
column24: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Defender [[Sol Campbell]], returning from injury praised the team performance in his post-match interview: ""It's brilliant for us. It's also great for the manager Arsène Wenger to get to the final in France – I'm sure he will get a great reception.""<ref>{{cite news

column5: The Arsenal pennant used in the quarter-final, second leg against Liverpool in April 2008.]]

column1: In the final against Barcelona, Lehmann was sent off in 18th minute for a professional foul on striker [[Samuel Eto'o]].<ref name=""barcaf"">{{cite news
column7: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Wenger reacted by substituting [[Robert Pirès]] for goalkeeper [[Manuel Almunia]], thus altering the formation.<ref name=""barcaf"" /> In spite of the disadvantage, Arsenal took the lead in the 37th minute, after Henry's free kick was headed in by Campbell.<ref name=""barcaf"" /> Henry missed a chance in the second half to give Arsenal a two-nil lead before Eto'o equalised with 14 minutes left.<ref name=""barcaf"" /> Substitute [[Henrik Larsson]] set up [[Juliano Belletti]] to score the winner for Barcelona.<ref name=""barcaf"" /> Wenger criticised referee [[Terje Hauge]] for sending off Lehmann, a view shared by club captain Henry and FIFA president [[Sepp Blatter]].<ref>{{cite news

column1: As Arsenal finished fourth in the league, in the [[2006–07 UEFA Champions League
column2: following season]] the club needed to play a third qualifying round, against [[NK Dinamo Zagreb
column3: Dinamo Zagreb]] in order to participate in the Champions League group stages. The team won 1–5 on aggregate, including a 3–0 victory in the first European match at the [[Emirates Stadium]].<ref>{{cite news
column9: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal was eliminated in the Round of 16 stage, losing on the away goal ruling to PSV Eindhoven.<ref>{{cite news
column10: title=Wretched Arsenal stare at a bleak future
column17: accessdate=26 May 2012 }}</ref> In the [[2007-08 UEFA Champions League
column18: 2007–08]] season, Arsenal equalled their biggest home win in European football, scoring seven against Slavia Prague.<ref>{{cite news
column26: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> The club beat holders Milan in the subsequent round, earning critical acclaim for their style of football, not least from [[Marcello Lippi]]: ""It would be good for football if Arsenal could win. They play on the ground, they manoeuvre the ball, very, very well. It's very fast and very technical.""<ref>{{cite news
column27: title=Arsenal the purists' pick for Europe win, says Lippi
column36: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> At the quarter-final stage, [[Liverpool F.C.
column37: Liverpool]] defeated Arsenal 5–3 on aggregate to set up a semi-final tie against Chelsea.<ref>{{cite news

column1: Arsenal progressed past the group stages of the [[2008–09 UEFA Champions League
column2: 2008–09]] Champions League season and beat Roma and Villarreal to face [[Manchester United F.C.
column3: Manchester United]] in the semi-finals.<ref>{{cite news
column11: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> A 1–0 defeat at [[Old Trafford]] meant Arsenal needed to win by two clear goals to progress, but goals from [[Park Ji-Sung]] and [[Cristiano Ronaldo]] in the first eleven minutes ended the club's chances of reaching the [[2009 UEFA Champions League Final]].<ref>{{cite news
column19: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Wenger in his post-match press conference described the match as ""the most disappointing night of my career"", adding ""I felt the fans were really up for a big night and to disappoint people who stand behind the team so much hurts.""<ref>{{cite news
column25: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal lost to holders Barcelona 5–3 on aggregate in the quarter-finals [[2009–10 UEFA Champions League
column26: the following season]], and in spite of beating the Spanish club 2–1 at the Emirates Stadium in [[2010–11 UEFA Champions League
column27: 2010–11]], Arsenal again were eliminated, this time at the Round of 16.<ref>{{cite news
column50: date=6 March 2012
column51: accessdate=27 May 2012 }}</ref> Arsenal exited at the same stage of the competition for the second consecutive season, against Milan. Having lost the away leg 4–0, the team gave a valiant performance in the second leg at home, winning 3–0 on the night, but unable to find the final goal that would have taken the game to extra time.

column1: '''''Stonehearst Asylum''''', previously known as '''''Eliza Graves''''', is an American [[thriller film]] directed by [[Brad Anderson (director)
column2: Brad Anderson]] and written by [[Joseph Gangemi]], loosely based on the short story ""[[The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether]]""<ref>[http://screenrant.com/eliza-graves-edgar-allan-poe-kate-beckinsale/ Kate Beckinsale in Talks for Edgar Allan Poe Adaptation ‘Eliza Graves’]</ref> by [[Edgar Allan Poe]]. The film, starring [[Kate Beckinsale]], [[Jim Sturgess]], [[Michael Caine]], [[Ben Kingsley]], and [[David Thewlis]], was released on October 24, 2014.

column1: <!-- Per [[WP:FILMPLOT]], plot summaries should be between 400 and 700 words. -->

In 1899, an Oxford University professor demonstrates a case of [[female hysteria]], Eliza Graves ([[Kate Beckinsale]]), before his class. Though she protests that she is sane, the professor points out that all mental patients claim to be sane, much as all criminals claim to be innocent. The professor advises his students to believe nothing they hear and only half of what they see. Later, a young man arrives at Stonehearst Asylum, where he desires to take up residency. A group of armed men led by Mickey Finn ([[David Thewlis]]) allow him entry. Finn escorts him to the office of the superintendent, Dr. Silas Lamb ([[Ben Kingsley]]), where the young doctor introduces himself as Dr. Edward Newgate ([[Jim Sturgess]]) from Oxford. Although Lamb was not expecting him, despite Newgate having sent letters preceding his arrival, he welcomes the help of an Oxford-educated doctor.

Newgate is surprised by Lamb's unorthodox methods. Lamb says that he does not believe in drugging or incarcerating his patients, and he encourages their delusions when he feels it will bring them greater happiness. Newgate becomes infatuated with Graves, now a resident at Stonehearst, when introduced to her. Lamb explains that Graves is a beautiful woman with an abused and painful past. She was raped and molested by her then-fiancé who had an ""appetite"" and got hysteria. One night, after their engagement, unable to control his lust, Charles Graves threw himself onto Eliza and tried to force her into sodomy. However, she resisted him, stabbing him in the right eye with a fork and biting his left ear. Hence, her father became angered and threw her into the asylum after forcing her to marry her ""monster"", who has since been trying to free her. Though she brushes aside his attempts at flirtation, she is struck by his humility and respectful demeanor. A fancy feast follows, during which the staff and patients mingle. Newgate and Finn argue, and, as a truce, Finn proposes a toast. Before Newgate can drink it, Graves causes him to spill his drink. As she helps him to clean up, Graves quietly insists that he flee the asylum, but Newgate refuses to leave without her.

Hearing a strange noise coming from the heating vent in his room, Newgate goes to investigate the boiler room. In the basement, he finds a large number of imprisoned people begging him for help. Initially believing them to be delirious patients, Edward starts to leave, only to be stopped by one of them shouting his name, having read the letters Lamb claimed they had not received. The prisoners reveal that they are the actual staff of Stonehearst, and the doctors and nurses Newgate has met are actually patients. He meets the real superintendent, Dr. Benjamin Salt ([[Michael Caine]]), who explains that Lamb and Finn drugged their drinks and led a revolt. Dr. Salt and Mrs. Pike ([[Sinéad Cusack]]), the matron, warn Newgate that Lamb is a dangerous madman – a surgeon who murdered his patients during wartime. Salt tells him that, even if he were to release them, they would not be able to fight Lamb's armed men in their weakened state. Salt tells him instead to leave them in the cells and return to London for help. Other staff disagree and tell him to find the keys and free them. Newgate attempts to recruit Graves, but she declines to become involved and tells him of Salt's abuses. Two of the staff escape from the boiler room, but are hunted down and killed by Finn, who continues to grow more suspicious of Newgate. When Newgate sneaks into Lamb's office to retrieve Salt's notes, he overhears Lamb and Finn conspire to tie up loose ends by the New Year. This takes the form of electrical shock treatment, which Lamb forces Newgate to perform on Salt. When Salt suffers amnesia, Lamb proclaims him cured of his delusion that he is the true administrator.

During the New Year's celebration, Finn murders one of the young female patients, which Lamb brushes off as an accidental death. Convinced that something must be done, Newgate attempts to spike the celebratory champagne. He is caught by Finn, who then pulls a knife on Newgate. Newgate fights with Finn who falls into a coal bin and supposedly is crushed by more coal dumped on to him after Newgate pulls a lever. Finn appears as the revelers are about to drink the spiked champagne and warns them all not to drink it.

Lamb prepares Newgate for electric shock therapy. Before it begins, Newgate reveals to Graves that he came to the asylum to rescue her once he saw her at the Oxford demonstration. Lamb grants Newgate a final request: to see a picture of Graves that he keeps in his pocket. When the picture turns out to be one of Lamb's victims, the shock causes Lamb to stagger out of the room in a daze. Finn goes to pick up the electric prods and just before he electrocutes Newgate, Graves shoves the gurney Newgate is on and knocks Finn over. Graves picks up the electric prods and kills Finn, who catches fire. The fire then spreads as Graves leads the patients out of the building and Newgate leaves to find Lamb, who has now become near-comatose from the guilt over his actions. Flashbacks reveal that Lamb, under extreme pressure, executed his patients as a form of [[Coup de grâce

After they have rescued the others, as daylight breaks, Newgate again asks Graves to leave with him, but she says that she cannot be with him because he is sane and she is not. Newgate says that he is not sane, as he is madly in love with her, and he intimates that he has a secret to tell her.

Later, Graves' husband and the earlier Oxford professor arrive at the asylum. The professor asks for Mrs. Graves' release, but Mrs. Pike, who is now in charge, says that Newgate already released her. The professor reveals that he is actually Newgate, and the man they knew is an escaped mental patient. Mrs. Graves and the impostor Newgate are shown in Tuscany, Italy, where they are known as Dr. and Mrs. Lamb. The two dance happily and embrace in a beautiful garden.

column1: The film was released on August 16, 2013, and was a critical failure as well as a [[box office bomb]].

Adam Cassidy is a low-level inventor who works for a corporation run by Nicholas Wyatt. After being fired for insubordination, Adam uses the company's credit card to pay for [[bottle service]] for his friends at a club. Wyatt and his enforcer, Miles Meachum, blackmail Adam into becoming a corporate spy for Wyatt by threatening to have him arrested for fraud.

Adam is trained by Judith Bolton and infiltrates a company run by Wyatt's former mentor, Jock Goddard. He provides Goddard, who stole several of Wyatt's ideas, with an advanced software able to hack into cellphones, with potential military applications. FBI Agent Gamble interrogates Adam, revealing that three other employees of Wyatt who transferred to Goddard's company were found dead, but Adam ignores him.

Adam finds out Emma Jennings, a woman he met during the party, is the Director of Marketing of Goddard's company. He initiates a relationship with Emma in order to steal files about Goddard's upcoming projects. Wyatt threatens to kill Adam's father, Frank Cassidy, if Adam doesn't steal a revolutionary prototype cellphone developed by Goddard. Adam later finds out Meachum and Bolton are monitoring him, so he destroys the cameras in his apartment. In retaliation, Meachum runs over Adam's friend, Kevin, with a car, nearly killing him. Adam is given 48 hours to steal the prototype.

Adam uses Emma's thumbprint lifted from a spoon to gain security access to the company's vault. He is confronted there by Goddard, who intends to take over Wyatt's company with evidence that Adam was acting as Wyatt's spy. Emma finds out Adam used her. Adam recruits Kevin to help him. A meeting is set with Wyatt and Goddard, where it is revealed that Bolton has spied against Wyatt on Goddard's behalf. Both men speak of the crimes they have committed to sabotage each other's companies.

Adam has secretly used software to transmit their conversation to Kevin, whose computer recordings are turned over to the FBI. Goddard, Wyatt, Bolton and Meachum are arrested by Gamble, while Adam is released for contributing to the FBI's investigation. He reconciles with Emma and opens a small startup company in Brooklyn with Kevin and their friends.
Principal photography commenced on location in [[Philadelphia]] in July 2012, and returned for further filming at the end of November 2012.<ref>{{cite web
